result: Loss of β4 spectrin causes motor impairment and disrupts AIS structure. Nes-Cre;Sptbn4F/F mice show pronounced tremor, significantly worse rotarod performance, and significantly reduced AIS Nav channels and AnkG. Despite these reductions, AnkG retains its periodic spacing at the AIS as shown by STED microscopy.
evaluation: Claims C6, C7, C30-C34, and C37 are well-supported by behavioral data (Figure 1A), immunostaining quantification (Figure 1B,C), and STED microscopy (Figure 1D,E). The statistical significance is reported (p=0.0017 for rotarod, p<0.05 for AnkG and Nav channels), and appropriate controls are included. The STED data showing preserved AnkG periodicity is a notable finding that adds rigor to the structural characterization.

result: Nodes of Ranvier in β4 spectrin-deficient mice are rescued by β1 spectrin and AnkR. In Nes-Cre;Sptbn4F/F mice, CNS nodes in the corpus callosum retain appropriately clustered nodal Nav channels due to compensation by β1 spectrin and AnkR.
evaluation: Claims C35, C36, and C38 are supported by immunostaining data (Figure 1F-H) showing normal nodal Nav channel clustering and the presence of β1 spectrin and AnkR at nodes in β4 spectrin-deficient mice. This is consistent with prior work (Liu et al., 2020; Ho et al., 2014) and demonstrates domain-specific compensation mechanisms.

result: β1 spectrin expression is heterogeneous in cortical neurons, with high levels in PV(+) interneurons where it colocalizes with AnkR. In β4 spectrin-deficient mice, β1 spectrin is recruited to the AIS of β1-high neurons but not β1-low neurons.
evaluation: Claims C39-C45 are supported by immunostaining data (Figure 2A-E) showing differential β1 spectrin expression patterns and quantification of AIS localization. The data show that 89% of β1-high neurons are PV(+) (Figure 2B) and that β1 spectrin is recruited to the AIS in 70% of β1-high neurons in Nes-Cre;Sptbn4F/F mice (p<0.001, Figure 2E). Sample sizes are adequate (120-125 neurons counted).

result: Despite the presence of AIS β1 spectrin in β1-high neurons of β4 spectrin-deficient mice, β1 spectrin cannot compensate for loss of β4 spectrin. AIS Nav channels remain significantly reduced, and the density is comparable between β1-high and β1-low neurons.
evaluation: Claims C46, C47, and C4 are supported by quantitative immunostaining data (Figure 2F,G) showing that even in β1-high neurons with AIS β1 spectrin, Nav channel levels remain significantly reduced (p=0.018) and comparable to β1-low neurons. This demonstrates that β1 spectrin cannot functionally compensate at the AIS, unlike at nodes of Ranvier.

result: Loss of β1 spectrin has no discernible effect on CNS structure or function. Nes-Cre;SptbF/F mice show normal behavior, normal rotarod performance, and normal AIS structure with appropriate levels of AnkG, Nav channels, and β4 spectrin.
evaluation: Claims C8, C48-C52, C77, and C78 are supported by behavioral testing (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) and immunostaining data (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B-F) showing no significant differences between β1 spectrin-deficient and control mice. Statistical comparisons show p>0.05 for all measured parameters. This suggests β1 spectrin is dispensable when β4 spectrin is present.

result: AnkR is not located at the AIS in control or β4 spectrin-deficient mice, even in neurons expressing high levels of AnkR. This is because AnkR lacks the giant exon (GE) domain necessary for AIS localization, preventing β1 spectrin from compensating for loss of β4 spectrin at the AIS.
evaluation: Claims C53-C55, C5, C56, and C59 are supported by immunostaining data (Figures 2C, 3A,B) showing absence of AIS AnkR in both control and β4 spectrin-deficient mice, and by transfection experiments (Figure 3D,E) demonstrating that the GE domain is necessary and sufficient for AIS targeting. The quantification shows <5% of neurons have AIS AnkR regardless of genotype or AnkR expression level (Figure 3B).

result: Transfection experiments in hippocampal neurons demonstrate that only AnkG-270kDa-GFP is targeted to the AIS, while AnkR-GFP is not. However, introduction of the giant exon into AnkR (AnkR/G chimera-GFP) is sufficient for AIS targeting.
evaluation: Claims C57, C58, and C105 are supported by transfection and immunostaining data (Figure 3D,E) showing differential AIS targeting. Quantification shows AnkG-270kDa has an AIS/dendrite ratio of ~3, AnkR has a ratio of ~0.7, and the AnkR/G chimera has a ratio of ~2.2 (p<0.001 for comparisons, Figure 3E). This provides mechanistic insight into why AnkR cannot compensate at the AIS.

result: Mice lacking both β1 and β4 spectrin show exacerbated nervous system dysfunction compared to single knockouts. Nes-Cre;SptbF/F;Sptbn4F/F mice perform significantly worse on the rotarod (p<0.0001) and exhibit frequent interictal spike discharges (299-792/hour) and spontaneous generalized seizures (49-154/hour) that occur during behavioral arrest.
evaluation: Claims C9, C62, C64-C66, and C12 are supported by behavioral testing (Figure 4A), EEG recordings (Figure 4B-D), and video monitoring (Video 1). The data show statistically significant differences in rotarod performance and quantified seizure activity in both male and female mice. Sample sizes are adequate (N=3-7 mice per group), and appropriate controls are included.

result: Mice lacking both β1 and β4 spectrin have profound disruption of AIS Na+ channel clustering. Immunostaining shows significantly reduced AnkG and PanNav at the AIS in both PV(+) and PV(-) neurons.
evaluation: Claims C10 and C67 are supported by immunostaining data (Figure 4E,F) showing significant reductions in both AnkG and PanNav at the AIS (p<0.05 for all comparisons). The quantification includes both PV(+) and PV(-) neurons, demonstrating that the disruption is not cell-type specific. Sample sizes are adequate (37-50 AIS measured per group).

result: Mice lacking both β1 and β4 spectrin show progressive loss of nodal Na+ channels. Analysis of corpus callosum nodes shows the percentage of nodes with Nav channels decreases from ~95% at 3 months to ~60% at 6 months.
evaluation: Claims C11 and C69 are supported by immunostaining data at multiple time points (Figure 4G,H) showing progressive loss of nodal Nav channels. The quantification shows statistically significant differences at both 3 months (p=0.0152) and 6 months (p=0.0009). Sample sizes are adequate (345-377 nodes counted per group). This demonstrates that both AIS and nodes are affected in double knockout mice.

result: No increased neuronal cell death or neurodegeneration was observed in β1/β4 spectrin-deficient mice as indicated by antibodies against active caspase-3 or βAPP.
evaluation: Claim C68 states that no increased cell death or neurodegeneration was observed, but the data are not shown in the figures. While the authors state this was assessed by immunostaining, the absence of presented data makes it difficult to fully evaluate this negative result. Additional information about the methods, sample sizes, and quantification would strengthen this claim.

result: The worsened behavioral and functional phenotypes in β1/β4 spectrin-deficient mice reflect disruption of both AIS and nodes of Ranvier, demonstrating the importance of these excitable domains for proper nervous system function.
evaluation: Claims C70 and C71 are supported by the collective data from behavioral testing, EEG recordings, and immunostaining showing disruption of both AIS and nodes in double knockout mice. The conclusion that both domains are important for nervous system function is well-supported by the severe phenotype observed when both are disrupted compared to single knockouts.

result: Loss of β4 spectrin and failure of β1 spectrin to compensate causes AIS proteins to be far less stable than nodal proteins. This observation helps explain the phenotypes of human pathogenic SPTBN4 variants, as AIS proteins rely mainly on β4 spectrin.
evaluation: Claims C92, C93, and C97 are supported by the comparative data showing that AIS are disrupted in β4 spectrin-deficient mice while nodes are rescued by β1 spectrin and AnkR. The connection to human disease (Wang et al., 2018) is reasonable given the similar phenotypes. However, the claim about protein stability is inferred from the immunostaining data rather than directly measured.

result: The authors speculate that the stability of nodal proteins compared to AIS proteins depends on flanking paranodal domains enriched with α2/β2 spectrin cytoskeleton. This difference may be a consequence of myelin and the distinction between intrinsic AIS assembly mechanisms and extrinsic, glia-dependent node assembly mechanisms.
evaluation: Claims C94-C96 and C113 are explicitly speculative ("we speculate") and are not directly tested in this study. While the speculation is reasonable and supported by prior work (Amor et al., 2017), it represents a hypothesis rather than a demonstrated result. Testing this hypothesis would require additional experiments examining paranodal contributions to nodal stability.

result: β1 spectrin cannot compensate for AIS β4 spectrin, even in PV(+) cells expressing high levels of AnkR and β1 spectrin, because β1 spectrin is the preferential binding partner for AnkR, and AnkR cannot be recruited to the AIS.
evaluation: Claims C100, C101, and C56 are supported by the immunostaining data showing lack of compensation (Figure 2F,G), absence of AIS AnkR (Figure 3B), and citation to prior work on β1 spectrin-AnkR binding (Ho et al., 2014). The mechanistic explanation is well-supported by the experimental data and prior literature.

result: AIS lack the molecular flexibility of nodes in that they require AnkG and β4 spectrin, while nodes can assemble from both AnkG/β4 spectrin and AnkR/β1 spectrin. This is notable given that AIS are thought to be evolutionary precursors to nodes of Ranvier.
evaluation: Claims C112 and C111 are supported by the collective experimental data showing differential compensation mechanisms at AIS versus nodes. The evolutionary context (Hill et al., 2008) provides interesting framing, though the evolutionary claim itself is not tested here. The main conclusion about molecular flexibility is well-supported by the data.

result: Prior work showed that a hierarchy of spectrin cytoskeletal proteins maintains nodal Na+ channels, with β1 spectrin and AnkR compensating for loss of β4 spectrin at nodes. The current study shows this hierarchy does not function at AIS.
evaluation: Claims C1-C3, C23-C25 accurately represent prior work (Liu et al., 2020) and are supported by appropriate citations. The contrast with the current findings at AIS is clearly demonstrated by the experimental data in this manuscript. This provides important context for interpreting the current results.

result: AIS require AnkG for assembly and Nav channel clustering. AnkG recruits β4 spectrin to the AIS, and the enrichment of AnkG at AIS depends on its giant exon, which interacts with β4 spectrin, EB1/3, and NDEL1 to stabilize the AIS cytoskeleton and regulate trafficking. Giant AnkG also interacts with GABARAP to stabilize GABA receptors.
evaluation: Claims C102-C110 are supported by appropriate citations to prior work (Zhou et al., 1998; Yang et al., 2007; Jenkins et al., 2015; Leterrier et al., 2011; Kuijpers et al., 2016; Nelson et al., 2018). These claims provide important background and mechanistic context for understanding the current findings. The authors accurately represent the prior literature.

result: Human pathogenic variants of β4 spectrin cause severe motor axonal neuropathy but do not affect sensory neuron function, likely due to partial compensation by β1 spectrin. These differences suggest that an AIS may render neurons particularly susceptible to loss of spectrin cytoskeletons.
evaluation: Claims C27-C29, C60-C61 are supported by citation to Wang et al., 2018 and are consistent with the findings in this manuscript. The inference that AIS render neurons susceptible to spectrin loss is reasonable given the data, though the speculation about compensation in human disease (C61) is not directly tested.

result: β spectrins form periodic cytoskeletons in axons that protect against mechanical injury and serve as signaling platforms. Different β spectrins show distinct phenotypes when deleted: α2 and β2 spectrin loss causes degeneration, while β2 spectrin loss in sensory neurons causes channel mislocalization without degeneration. β4 spectrin also functions in signaling in cardiomyocytes.
evaluation: Claims C72-C76, C79-C85 are supported by appropriate citations to prior work (Xu et al., 2013; Huang et al., 2017a; Lorenzo et al., 2019; Ikeda et al., 2006; Liu and Rasband, 2019; Zhang et al., 2013; Hund et al., 2010; Unudurthi et al., 2018). These claims provide important context for understanding the diverse roles of spectrin proteins and accurately represent the prior literature.

result: Previous studies on β4 spectrin mutant mice relied on truncated forms of the protein and did not examine contributions from other β spectrins or determine if nodal defects were secondary to AIS disruption.
evaluation: Claims C86-C89 accurately describe limitations of prior studies (Komada and Soriano, 2002; Yang et al., 2004) and provide justification for the current experimental approach using conditional knockout mice. This contextualizes the novelty and importance of the current work.

result: One report indicated β2 spectrin may be found at AIS in cultured hippocampal neurons, but even if present in vivo, it cannot compensate for loss of β4 spectrin.
evaluation: Claims C98 and C99 are supported by citation to Lazarov et al., 2018 and by the experimental data showing AIS disruption in β4 spectrin-deficient mice despite potential β2 spectrin presence. The conclusion that β2 spectrin cannot compensate is well-supported by the data.

result: Background claims about spectrin structure, prior findings on spectrin function at AIS and nodes, and mechanisms of AIS versus node assembly.
evaluation: These claims (C13-C22, C26, C90-C91, C115-C116) provide background context and are supported by appropriate citations to prior work. They accurately represent established knowledge and prior findings, providing necessary context for interpreting the current results.
